q: The low Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC) of fly ash is primarily attributed to:
solution: Fly Ash and CEC: Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC) is the ability of a material to retain and exchange cations (positively charged ions) in soil or substrate. Fly ash typically has low CEC because its particles are non-plastic, meaning they do not have clay-like properties that allow significant ion exchange. Non-plastic particles lack the layered structures and surface charges seen in clay minerals, which are responsible for higher CEC. Despite having some reactive oxides, the absence of plasticity limits the ability of fly ash to retain nutrients, making its CEC low.

q: Arrange the following in ascending order of their lime content percentage: A. Class F fly ash B. Class C fly ash C. Portland cement D. Quick lime
solution: Ascending Order of Lime Content: Class F Fly Ash (A) Class F fly ash is known as "low-calcium fly ash." Lime (Cao) content is generally less than 10%, usually in the range of 2-8%. Derived from burning anthracite or bituminous coal. Most of its pozzolanic properties come from silicates, not from lime reactivity. Class C Fly Ash (B) Called "high-calcium fly ash." Lime content typically ranges from 15% to over 30%. Produced by burning lignite or sub-bituminous coal. Higher self-cementing ability due to increased Cao content. Portland Cement (C) Lime (Cao) content in Portland cement is much higher than in fly ash-usually between 60-67%. Lime is the main ingredient promoting hardening and strength after hydration. The matrix is a blended product of lime and other oxides, not pure calcium oxide. Quick Lime (D) Quick lime is chemically pure calcium oxide (Cao). Lime content is generally more than 90% (often 95-99%). Used directly for rapid chemical reactions or as an activator in pozzolanic mixes. Highly caustic and reacts vigorously with water.

q: If a composting facility handles 150 t/day of organic waste with 60% moisture, how many tonnes of dry matter are processed daily?
solution: Explanation: Given data: Total organic waste handled = 150 t/day Moisture content = 60% = 0.60 Calculate the Dry Matter Fraction: The total mass consists of moisture and dry matter. Dry Matter Fraction = 1.00 - 0.60 = 0.40 Calculate Daily Dry Matter Processed: Dry Matter = Total Waste × Dry Matter Fraction Dry Matter = 150× 0.40 = 60 t/day Conclusion: Therefore, the composting facility processes 60 tonnes of dry matter per day.

q: Which of the following are methods for hazardous waste treatment? Management A. Solidification/stabilization B. Incineration C. Landfilling without liner D. Chemical neutralization
solution: Overview of Hazardous Waste Treatment: Hazardous waste treatment involves processes that change the physical, chemical, or biological characteristics of waste to minimize its harmful effects on human health and the environment. The goal is to detoxify, neutralize, or reduce the mobility of contaminants before final disposal. Statement A - Solidification/Stabilization - True: This process involves mixing waste with binding agents (like cement, lime, or fly ash) to reduce leaching of contaminants. It is commonly used for heavy metals and industrial sludge. Statement B - Incineration - True : High-temperature combustion destroys organic hazardous wastes and reduces their volume significantly. Specialized hazardous waste incinerators are designed to handle toxic substances with pollution control systems. Statement C - Landfilling without liner - False: Modern hazardous waste landfills must have liners, leachate collection systems, and environmental monitoring to prevent pollution. Disposing hazardous waste in unlined landfills can contaminate soil and groundwater. Statement D- Chemical Neutralization - True: This method uses chemical reactions to convert hazardous chemicals into less toxic or non-toxic substances. For example, acids can be neutralized with bases before disposal.

q: Given below are two statements: Statement I: Hazardous materials such as lead, mercury, and hexavalent chromium in one form or other are present in electronic wastes. Statement II: Landfilling of electronic waste is the best operation from the environmental viewpoint. In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is correct but Statement II is false
Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is true
solution: Concept: E-waste Definition: Electronic waste or "e-waste" refers to old, end-of-life electronic appliances like computers, laptops, TVs, and mobile phones. Analysis of Statement I (Correct): Electronic devices contain a multitude of toxic substances. For example, televisions and monitors typically contain lead, mercury, and cadmium, while circuit boards often contain nickel, beryllium, and hexavalent chromium. Analysis of Statement II (Incorrect): Landfilling is not the best environmental practice for e-waste. Because e-waste contains hazardous heavy metals, disposal in landfills can lead to these toxins leaching into the soil and groundwater, posing significant risks to human health and the environment. Alternative: Recycling and proper recovery of valuable materials are considered far more sustainable than landfilling.

q: Provision of Extended Producer's Responsibility (EPR) of producer, importer and brand owner for collecting back the waste generated by their product has been in the A. Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016 B. Construction & Demolition Waste Management Rules, 2016 C. Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 D. E-waste (Management) Rules, 2016 E. Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016 Choose the correct answer from the options given below
solution: · Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016: EPR is defined as the responsibility of producers of packaging products (plastic, tin, glass, etc.) for management until the end-of-life of the products. · Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016: The Ministry of Environment notified specific EPR guidelines to strengthen the circular economy and promote sustainable plastic packaging. · E-waste (Management) Rules, 2016: These rules utilize a collection mechanism-based approach (collection centers, take-back systems) involving Producers and Producer Responsibility Organizations (PROs) under the EPR framework. · Note on Construction & Demolition (C&D) Rules: While these rules mandate that generators segregate waste and hand it over to authorized facilities to prevent littering, they do not establish a formal EPR "collect back" system for the producer in the same manner as the other three rules. · Note on Biomedical Rules: These rules focus on segregation and treatment by the generator/facility rather than EPR-based collection by the original product manufacturer.

q: Which one of the following are four major waste types identified based on Physical characteristics? A. Solid Waste B. Sludge and Slurry Waste C. Combustible Waste D. Reactive Waste E. Waste Water Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A, B, C and D only
A, B, C and E only
B, C, D and E only
solution: Solid Waste (A): Any discarded material abandoned by disposal, burning, or recycling. Sludge and Slurry (B): Wet mixtures of liquid and solid components (sludge is thick; slurry is thin) produced from treatment processes. Combustible Waste (C): Material capable of burning or incineration, excluding explosives. Waste Water (E): Water generated after freshwater or saline water has been used in deliberate applications. Why D is excluded: Reactive Waste is categorized based on chemical properties (such as the tendency to explode or create toxic fumes) rather than its physical state.

solution: Concept- Electronic waste or e-waste is one of the emerging problems in developed and developing countries worldwide. q: A landfill should not be constructed within how many meters (m) of a lake or pond?
solution: · Distance Requirement: Landfills must not be constructed within 200 m of a lake or pond. · Technical Reason: This buffer zone is required due to environmental concerns regarding the runoff of wastewater (leachate) that has come into contact with the waste, which could contaminate the water body. · Related Siting Standard: For inhabited areas, a larger zone of 500 m around the landfill boundary must be declared a "No-Development Buffer Zone."

q: Which of the following has a maximum share in 'E-waste'?
solution: Electronic waste or e-waste is a term used to describe electronic products that have reached the end of their useful life and are discarded, including electronic equipment such as computers, mobile phones, televisions, and other electronic devices. These electronic devices contain hazardous materials that can be harmful to human health and the environment if not disposed of properly. Medical Equipment: Medical equipment, such as x-ray machines and MRI scanners, contains hazardous materials, but it has a relatively small share in e-waste compared to other electronic devices. Medical equipment is also usually managed and disposed of through specialized processes to minimize the risks associated with hazardous materials. Solar Waste: Solar panels contain hazardous materials and can contribute to e-waste, but they have a longer lifespan compared to other electronic devices. The recycling of solar panels is still a developing field, and the share of solar waste in e-waste is relatively small. Computer Waste: Computers and other electronic devices are one of the largest contributors to e-waste globally. Due to rapid technological advancements, computers and other electronic devices quickly become obsolete, leading to frequent replacements and discards. The hazardous materials in electronic devices can pose significant environmental and health risks if not disposed of properly. Telephone Waste: Mobile phones and telephones are also significant contributors to e-waste. With the increasing popularity of smartphones and their short life cycles, the share of telephone waste in e-waste is expected to increase. However, the overall share of telephone waste in e-waste is relatively small compared to computer waste.

q: Identify the non-recyclable wastes among the following: (A) Paper (B) Plastic bottles (C) Tharmocol (D) Tetra packs (E) Metal
solution: (A) Paper - Paper is generally a recyclable material. However, some types of paper are not recyclable, such as paper coated with wax or plastic Additionally, paper products that are contaminated with food, liquids, or other substances may not be able to be recycled. (B) Plastic bottles - Plastic bottles are technically recyclable, but the reality is that many plastic bottles end up in landfills or the environment. LDPE plastic, also known as Low-Density Polyethylene, falls among the non-recyclable plastics category. This plastic is made of soft, flexible, and lightweight material often used to prepare wash bottles, tubes, plastic bags, computer parts, and many others. Several countries have banned plastic bags because it's the most common form of pollution (C) Tharmocol - Tharmocol, also known as expanded polystyrene foam, is a type of plastic foam that is non-biodegradable and non-recyclable. It is often used in packaging and insulation, but it can take hundreds of years to decompose in a landfill. While some recycling programs exist for thermocouples, they are not widely available and are not able to handle large quantities of the material. (D) Tetra packs - Tetra packs, or aseptic packages, are commonly used for packaging food and beverages such as milk, juice, and soup. However, they are generally not recyclable due to their complex layering of plastic, aluminum, and paper. While some recycling programs exist for tetra packs, they are not widely available and are not able to handle large quantities of the material.

Food waste, manures and waste from producing crops are biodegradable solid waste.. Non-biodegradable solid waste- also sometimes called inorganic solid wastes) are those that do not decompose by microbial action. These wastes include plastic containers, scrap metal, food and drink cans and plastic bags.

solution: Explanation: Oily sludge is a hazardous waste generated from petrochemical processes that requires careful management and disposal .

q: Which international agreement governs the transboundary movement of hazardous waste and its disposal?
solution: Explanation: The Basel Convention is the primary international treaty that controls the transboundary movement of hazardous wastes, particularly from developed to less developed countries.

q: Under the Basel Convention, what is generally prohibited regarding the transboundary movement of hazardous waste?
solution: Explanation: Many countries, including India, prohibit the import of hazardous waste for final disposal under regulations that align with the Basel Convention. Import is generally restricted to recycling, recovery, and reuse.

q: In India, which entity is responsible for granting authorization to facilities that handle, generate, or transport hazardous waste?
options: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF , CC)
State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) / Pollution Control Committee (PCC)
solution: Explanation: While the CPCB sets nationwide guidelines, the SPCBs and PCCs are responsible for implementing these rules and granting authorizations to facilities within their respective states or union territories.

q: Which of the following is an example of universal waste?
solution: Explanation: Universal wastes are a special category of hazardous waste that are commonly generated by a wide variety of businesses and households and are subject to less stringent regulations. Examples include batteries, fluorescent bulbs, and mercury-containing equipment

q: A waste with a flash point below 60°C (140°F) is classified as which type of hazardous waste?
solution: Explanation: Ignitable hazardous wastes are those that can easily catch fire at relatively low temperatures, often indicated by a flash point below 60°C.

q: Which of the following is a common method for the disposal of low-level radioactive waste?
solution: Explanation : While not applicable to all radioactive waste, low-level radioactive waste is often disposed of in special, securely engineered landfills after proper treatment. High-level radioactive waste requires more complex and long-term storage methods .

q: Under Indian rules, who is responsible for the safe disposal of hazardous waste?
solution: Explanation: Similar to the RCRA's "cradle-to-grave" principle, Indian hazardous waste regulations hold the generator of the waste responsible for its proper and safe disposal.

q: What is the purpose of a liner system and leachate collection system in a secure landfill?
options: To generate methane gas for energy
To speed up the decomposition of organic material
solution: Explanation: Secure landfills for hazardous waste are designed with multiple protective layers, including liners, to contain the hazardous waste and prevent the toxic liquid (leachate) from contaminating the underlying soil and groundwater.

q: In hazardous waste management, what is the primary purpose of a solidification/stabilization process?
options: To increase the volume of the waste for easier transport.
To break down toxic organic compounds.
To reduce the mobility of hazardous contaminants.
solution: Explanation: Solidification involves adding a reagent to the waste to solidify it, while stabilization involves a chemical reaction to immobilize or bind the hazardous components. Both processes are designed to reduce the risk of contaminants leaching into the environment.

q: According to the EIA Notification 2006, "Category A" projects require Environmental Clearance from:
options: State Level Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA)
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC)
solution: Under the EIA Notification, 2006 , developmental projects are classified into Category 'A' and Category 'B'. Category 'A' projects (large-scale with significant impact) require Environmental Clearance (EC) from the Central Government, i.e., the MoEF&CC . Category 'B' projects require clearance from the State Level Environment Impact Assessment Authority (SEIAA).

q: Which of the following is the correct chronological sequence of stages in the Environmental Clearance process?
solution: The correct chronological order of the EC process as per the EIA Notification, 2006 is: Screening: Determining whether the project requires EIA (Only for Category B). Scoping: Determining the Terms of Reference (ToR) for the EIA study. Public Consultation: Gathering concerns from local affected persons. Appraisal: Detailed scrutiny of the EIA report by the Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC) or State Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC).

q: In the EIA process, "Screening" is required for:
options: Category B projects to determine if they are B1 or B2
solution: Category 'A' projects mandate an EIA, so they do not need screening. Category 'B' projects undergo Screening at the state level to decide if they require a full EIA ( Category B1 ) or are exempt from the EIA study ( Category B2 ).

q: Under the Plastic Waste Management Rules (as amended), what is the minimum mandated thickness for plastic carry bags (effective from Dec 31, 2022)?
solution: The Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2021 increased the minimum thickness of plastic carry bags in phases to facilitate collection and recycling: From 50 to 75 microns (effective Sept 30, 2021). From 75 to 120 microns (effective December 31, 2022 ).

q: Projects classified as "Category B2" are exempted from which stage of the EC process?
solution: Projects classified as Category B2 are considered to have a lower environmental impact. Therefore, they are exempted from the Scoping stage (no detailed ToR needed) and the Public Consultation stage. They are appraised based on the application (Form-1) and Pre-Feasibility Report (PFR) alone.

q: Under the Construction and Demolition (C&D) Waste Management Rules, 2016, large generators must segregate waste into:
options: 4 streams: Concrete/Masonry, Steel/Metal, Wood/Plastic, and Soil
solution: According to Rule 4 of the Construction and Demolition (C&D) Waste Management Rules, 2016 , large generators (who generate more than 20 tons/day or 300 tons/month) must segregate waste into four specific streams: Concrete, soil, masonry, and mortar. Wood and plastics. Steel and other metals. Other construction wastes. Note: "Soil" often falls into the first category, but the most distinct option listing multiple streams is (c).

q: The "Generic Structure of Environmental Impact Assessment Document" is provided in which Appendix of the EIA Notification 2006?
solution: Appendix III of the EIA Notification, 2006 outlines the "Generic Structure of Environmental Impact Assessment Document," detailing the chapters (Introduction, Project Description, Baseline Data, Impact Assessment, EMP, etc.) required in the EIA report. Appendix I is Form-1. Appendix II is Form-1A. Appendix III A lists standard ToR.

q: As per the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016, "Liquid Pathological Waste" should be treated by:
options: Chemical disinfection followed by discharge into drains
solution: According to the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016 , Liquid Pathological Waste (generated from labs, washing, cleaning, etc.) must be segregated at source and pre-treated (usually via chemical disinfection or neutralization) before mixing with other wastewater. It is then drained into the sewer system leading to a Sewage Treatment Plant (STP) or Effluent Treatment Plant (ETP). It is not incinerated or buried.

q: Which Act empowers the Central Government to take all necessary measures for "protecting and improving the quality of the environment"?
options: The Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
solution: This act is known as the "Umbrella Act." Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act (EPA), 1986 empowers the Central Government to take all necessary measures to protect and improve the quality of the environment and prevent, control, and abate environmental pollution.

q: A "Silence Zone" under the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules is defined as an area within 100 meters around:
solution: The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 defines a "Silence Zone" as an area comprising not less than 100 meters around hospitals, educational institutions, courts, religious places, or any other area declared as such by the competent authority.

q: The validity of Environmental Clearance (EC) for "River Valley Projects" is currently:
solution: As per recent amendments to the EIA Notification 2006 (specifically the March 2021 amendment and subsequent clarifications): The validity of EC for River Valley Projects has been extended to 10 years (previously 10, then extended to 13 in some contexts during COVID, but 10 is the standard baseline period now compared to the older 5 or 7 years). Note: Mining projects can have up to 30 years.

q: Under the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, the term "EPR" applies to:
options: Producers (including importers) of all types of batteries
solution: The Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 replaced the 2001 rules. They apply to all types of batteries (Lead-acid, Li-ion, Ni-Cd, etc.) regardless of chemistry or use (EV, portable, industrial, automotive). The concept of Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) mandates that Producers (including manufacturers and importers) are responsible for the collection and recycling/refurbishment of waste batteries.

q: Which form is used for the "Application for Environmental Clearance" under the EIA Notification 2006?
solution: Form 1: General application form for EC for most projects. Form 1A: Specific checklist for construction projects (Item 8 of the Schedule). Since construction projects are a major part of EC applications, both forms are standard application documents under the notification.

q: The "Fly Ash Notification" mandates that all coal/lignite-based thermal power plants must achieve 100% fly ash utilization within:
solution: The MoEF&CC issued a notification (Dec 2021) regarding fly ash utilization. For new coal/lignite-based thermal power plants, 100% fly ash utilization must be achieved within 4 years of commissioning. Existing legacy plants have different timelines (e.g., 3-5 years based on their utilization percentage).

q: "Public Hearing" is NOT required for which of the following projects?
options: Projects located within notified Industrial Estates/Parks
solution: Under Clause 7(iii) of the EIA Notification 2006, Public Hearing is exempted for: Projects located within Industrial Estates or Parks (specifically those notified by the Government prior to 2006 or those that have already obtained EC). Modernization of irrigation projects. Expansion of Roads/Highways (if no land acquisition). Building/Construction projects (Area Development).
